title: Area IV review: Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
intro: These questions mix all eight Tasks of Area IV: normal, soft-field and short-field takeoffs and landings, forward slips and go-arounds. Many are real-world scenarios that join two Tasks, just like the checkride.

questions.q: Your POH gives no approach speeds, and VSO is 45 knots. Using the AFH targets, which pair of speeds fits the base leg and final approach?
options: Base about 63 knots, final about 59 knots
Base about 54 knots, final about 59 knots, speeding up on the way in
Base 59 knots, final 63 knots
Base about 68 knots, final about 63 knots, using 1.5 and 1.4 times VSO
questions.why: On base, the AFH targets about 1.4 VSO: 1.4 x 45 = 63 knots [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. With no manufacturer's speed, final uses 1.3 VSO: 1.3 x 45 = 58.5, about 59 knots [[24:174|AFH 9-3]]. You slow down from base to final, not the other way around.

questions.q: Your POH shows a 790-foot takeoff ground run at 5,000 feet pressure altitude on a standard day. Today it is 20 °C warmer than standard. What does the PHAK example say to expect?
options: Density altitude above 7,000 feet, but the same 790-foot run since the POH figure is for pressure altitude
Density altitude of 5,000 feet, so the run is still 790 feet
Density altitude below 5,000 feet, and a shorter run
Density altitude above 7,000 feet, and a ground run closer to 1,000 feet
questions.why: Warm air expands and raises the density altitude to above 7,000 feet, so the ground run may be closer to 1,000 feet [[1:260|PHAK 11-4]]. That is why you work out takeoff distance from the POH for today's conditions, every time [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].

questions.q: You are flying a forward slip to a landing with the flaps up. Where does the AFH say to bring the power to idle?
options: On short final, once the slip is set up
Abeam the landing point on the downwind leg
At the start of the downwind leg
On base leg, right after the turn from downwind
questions.why: When abeam the landing point on downwind, reduce power to idle and start down. If you are not coming down fast enough, slip on downwind or base, and make coordinated turns to base and final [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

questions.q: The Chart Supplement shows that a grass strip slopes uphill toward the north. You will land to the north now and take off to the north later. What should you expect?
options: A longer landing roll and a shorter takeoff run, because the slope helps you speed up toward the north
No change, since slope only matters on pavement
A shorter landing roll and a shorter takeoff run
A shorter landing roll, but a longer takeoff run
questions.why: An upsloping runway usually shortens the landing roll, but it slows acceleration and lengthens the takeoff run [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. On a soft field you should avoid using the brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], so the uphill slope helps you stop. Plan the departure for the longer roll.

questions.q: At a towered airport you want to take off from an intersection instead of the end of the runway. What does the AIM say?
options: You must check that the runway left past the intersection is long enough for your takeoff
You may not ask for an intersection takeoff; you must use the full runway
The tower checks that the remaining runway is long enough for your takeoff, so you need not check it yourself
Intersection takeoffs are only for airplanes with short-field charts
questions.why: Pilots must check an intersection during preflight planning. The minimum runway needed for takeoff must fit within the reduced runway length and reduced declared distances. On request, controllers give the distance from the intersection to the runway end, rounded down to the nearest 50 feet [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10]].

questions.q: How does the soft-field takeoff roll differ from the short-field takeoff roll?
options: Soft field: nose wheel kept on the ground until VY so the tires stay planted. Short field: nose held high from the start to unload the mains
Soft field: nose held high early so the wings take the weight. Short field: full weight on the mains in a low-drag attitude until near VX
Both hold the nose high from the start of the roll
Both keep full weight on the wheels until VX
questions.why: On a soft field, hold a nose-high attitude as early as possible to move the weight from the wheels to the wings [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. On a short field, roll with full weight on the main wheels in a low-drag attitude [[24:143|AFH 6-11]], then rotate to the VX attitude as VX approaches [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

questions.q: Use the Cessna 172R chart. You land at sea level, 30 °C, no wind, on pavement, but the flaps won't extend. Using the chart notes, what approach speed and total distance over a 50-foot obstacle should you plan?
options: 62 KIAS and about 1,809 feet
69 KIAS and 1,340 feet
69 KIAS and about 1,809 feet
69 KIAS and about 1,474 feet
questions.why: The chart gives 1,340 feet at sea level and 30 °C, based on 62 KIAS at 50 feet. Note 4: with flaps up, add 7 KIAS (62 + 7 = 69) and allow 35% more distance: 1,340 x 1.35 = about 1,809 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. With no flaps, a forward slip is a useful way to come down steeper without gaining speed [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: You go around in a retractable-gear airplane and circle back to land. Before the next approach, what does the AFH stress?
options: Do the entire before-landing checklist again
Re-check only the flaps, since the rest was done the first time
Skip the checklist so your eyes stay outside
Re-check only the items you changed during the go-around
questions.why: If you return to land, re-do the entire before-landing checklist. A go-around breaks your habit pattern, which is a classic setup for a gear-up landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

questions.q: In the round out, a student stares at the runway just in front of the nose. What does the AFH say tends to happen?
options: Flying into the runway nose first
Rounding out too high and dropping the airplane in
Floating far down the runway with extra speed
Touching down on the nose wheel only
questions.why: Focusing too close blurs the view, so reactions are abrupt or late; pilots tend to over-control, round out high and drop it in. Focusing too far ahead can lead to flying into the ground nose first [[24:178|AFH 9-7]]. Move your eyes slowly from just over the nose to the touchdown zone and back [[24:178|AFH 9-7]], and start the round out about 10 to 20 feet up [[24:179|AFH 9-8]].

questions.q: You are ready for takeoff when you hear that a microburst was reported just off the departure end a few minutes ago. Which fact from the PHAK helps you decide what to do?
options: A microburst usually lasts about 5 to 15 minutes, so waiting it out is a good option
Their downdrafts are under 500 fpm, so a trainer can climb through one
They start with a tailwind, so the danger is only during the takeoff roll
Microbursts usually last about an hour, so cancel the flight and wait for the next weather update
questions.why: A typical microburst is 1 to 2 miles across and lasts about 5 to 15 minutes, with downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30 to 90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. That is far more than a trainer can climb against. Taking off into one, you meet a headwind first, then the downdraft and a growing tailwind [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

questions.q: You are ending a forward slip on short final. What is the right way to take it out?
options: Level the wings and smoothly release the rudder together, while setting the normal glide attitude
Keep the rudder in and level the wings with aileron only
Release the rudder all at once, then level the wings, because the slip ends the moment the pedal is freed
Add power first, then level the wings
questions.why: Level the wings and at the same time release the rudder while you set the normal glide attitude. If you let go of the rudder abruptly, the nose swings into line too fast and the airplane tends to pick up extra speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

questions.q: You are about to depart a private grass strip with no windsock. Leaves and small twigs are moving all the time, and a light flag is extended. About how strong is the wind?
options: Less than 1 knot
1 to 3 knots
7 to 10 knots
22 to 27 knots
questions.why: The AIM table says leaves and small twigs constantly moving, with light flags extended, means about 7 to 10 knots. At 1 to 3 knots, smoke drift shows the direction but wind vanes stay still [[34:227|AIM TBL 10-2-3]]. Learn to read the wind from smoke, dust and other clues when there is no windsock [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

questions.q: Grass strip check: the runway is dry grass at sea level, it is 20 °C, the wind is calm, and the airplane weighs 2,000 pounds. Reading the sample takeoff table and its notes, about how far until you are 50 feet up?
options: 1,110 feet
About 1,277 feet
About 1,201 feet
About 696 feet
questions.why: The 2,000-pound row at sea level and 20 °C shows 605 feet of ground roll and 1,110 feet total. Note 3 says add 15% of the ground roll figure for dry grass: 0.15 x 605 = about 91 feet, so 1,110 + 91 = about 1,201 feet [[1:278|PHAK 11-22]]. About 1,277 feet wrongly takes 15% of the total, and about 696 feet is the new ground roll alone.

questions.q: You just landed with full flaps on a muddy grass strip and are still rolling slowly. When should you raise the flaps?
options: Right away, to put more weight on the wheels and improve braking on the soft surface while you are still rolling
Right away, to keep mud off them
Before the nose wheel touches, to help hold it off
Not during the rollout; later, when clear and stopped, after you positively identify the flap control
questions.why: On a soft field, raising the flaps during the after-landing roll is generally unwise: keeping full control of the airplane matters more [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. Do the after-landing checklist once clear and stopped, and positively identify the flap control first. Pilots have raised the gear instead of the flaps while still rolling [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

questions.q: Halfway down final, the picture shows you too high while the airspeed reads 8 knots below target. Power is where you normally set it. Which control fixes this, per the AFH energy rules?
options: Start a forward slip to get rid of the extra height while holding the same airspeed
Add power, since you are slow
Raise the nose to slow your descent
Use the elevator: lower the nose to trade the extra height for speed
questions.why: Higher and slower is an energy distribution error: the total energy is about right but in the wrong place, so fix it with the elevator by trading altitude for airspeed. When altitude and speed are off in the same direction, that is a total energy error, fixed with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. A slip removes energy you need here [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: On a short-field approach you have just passed over the trees at the end of the field, with full flaps set at the right point. How should you handle the power?
options: Reduce power slightly over the obstacle, then slowly reduce it; don't chop it
Close the throttle right away so you don't float, then flare from the glide with power at idle
Add power to get back on a normal glide path
Hold the same power all the way to touchdown
questions.why: Over the obstacle you may reduce power slightly, and with full flaps at the right point you can then slowly reduce power [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Cutting power to idle too early in the round out is a listed error that leads to a hard landing [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

questions.q: You are established on final at a non-towered airport. Another airplane, lower than you, turns a short base ahead of you and will cut in front. Who has the right-of-way?
options: The other airplane, because it is lower and two airplanes approaching to land give the lower one priority
The other airplane, because it is closer to the runway
Whoever calls final first on CTAF
You do: the lower airplane may not use its altitude to cut in front of an airplane on final
questions.why: An airplane on final has the right-of-way over other aircraft in flight. When two airplanes are approaching to land, the lower one has the right-of-way, but it may not use that rule to cut in front of an airplane on final or to overtake it [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Still, avoiding the collision comes first: overtaking another airplane is a good reason to go around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

questions.q: After a soft-field lift-off you accelerate in ground effect to VX, then start to climb out of it. What should you be ready for?
options: The nose tends to drop, so you need more back pressure
The nose tends to pitch up, and induced drag goes up
Induced drag drops further, so the airplane speeds up
The airspeed indicator starts to read lower
questions.why: Climbing out of ground effect, the airplane needs more angle of attack, has more induced drag and needs more thrust, and tends to pitch up, needing less elevator. The airspeed indicator reads higher, not lower [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Not expecting the pitch-up is a listed soft-field error [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

questions.q: Your engine quits at 800 feet after takeoff. You are gliding to a field ahead but are too high. Your POH limits slips to 30 seconds to prevent fuel starvation. What does the AFH say about that limit now?
options: It still applies, so use only short slips and watch the fuel quantity until you are sure of making the field
It does not matter in a real engine-out emergency, unless a long slip caused the engine problem
Slips are never allowed after an engine failure
It means you should turn back to the runway instead
questions.why: Slip limits by time or fuel quantity prevent fuel starvation in uncoordinated flight. In an actual engine-out emergency the limit is irrelevant, unless a long slip caused the engine problem [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. A slip starts faster than lowering flaps and can be removed without penalty [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

questions.q: On a short-field takeoff, a student holds the airplane on the runway with forward elevator pressure until VX. What problem does the AFH warn about?
options: A strong pitch-up the moment the wheels leave the ground
A lift-off at too low an airspeed
Too much weight on the nose wheel, possible wheelbarrowing, and slower acceleration
Too little rudder authority to stay on the centerline, because the nose wheel is doing the steering for you
questions.why: Holding the airplane on the ground with forward elevator puts too much pressure on the nose wheel, may cause wheelbarrowing, and hurts acceleration. If it wants to fly early, let it lift off, then level off with the wheels just clear of the runway until VX [[24:144|AFH 6-12]].

questions.q: After a normal takeoff you are climbing at VY with full power. When does the AFH recommend reducing to climb power?
options: As soon as the flaps are up
At a safe maneuvering altitude, at least 500 feet above the surrounding terrain or obstacles
Right after lift-off, to protect the engine
At 200 feet AGL, once past the runway end
questions.why: Keep takeoff power until at least 500 feet above the surrounding terrain or obstacles. VY and full power give the most altitude in the least time, and that height gives you options if the engine fails. At a safe maneuvering altitude, set climb power and trim [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

questions.q: Compare two landings: a soft grass strip with open fields before it, and a short field with tall trees on the approach. How should the soft-field approach differ?
options: Fly it faster than the short-field approach, for extra energy in the float
Use the same final speed, and make it steeper to touch down sooner
Make it a power-off glide so the wheels touch gently
Use the same final speed, but no steep descent is needed since there are no obstacles
questions.why: The short-field final approach speed also fits soft fields, and there is no reason for a steep descent unless obstacles are in the path [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Over obstacles, a slightly steeper approach puts touchdown closer to them and leaves more room to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. A soft-field landing keeps some power on through touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

questions.q: You decide to go around and shove the throttle to full in one quick jab. What does the AFH say?
options: Abrupt power is best because it stops the descent faster and the engine always responds at once
Power should be smooth and positive; abrupt throttle movement can make some engines falter
Quick power cancels the left-turning tendency
Quick power makes the nose drop, so pull back hard
questions.why: Full power is your first concern, applied smoothly and without hesitation. Abrupt throttle movements cause some engines to falter. Turn carburetor heat off, if applicable. Expect the nose to rise and yaw left, and hold forward pressure and right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: Your home runway is narrow. Today's destination has a runway about twice as wide. What mistake does this set you up for if you miss the illusion?
options: Flying too low on final and landing short of the runway, as with a narrow runway
Touching down in a crab
Leveling off too high and landing hard, or overshooting
Flying too slow on final and stalling
questions.why: A narrower-than-usual runway makes you feel high, so you fly low. A wider-than-usual runway has the opposite effect: you may level out high and land hard or overshoot the runway [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

questions.q: On the checkride, the examiner picks the 1,000-foot markers as your touchdown point. You touch down 300 feet past them, aligned and with no drift. For which landings does that meet the ACS?
options: Normal, forward slip and short-field
Short-field only
Normal and forward slip to a landing, but not short-field
None of them
questions.why: Normal landings (ACS PA.IV.B.S10) and forward slips to a landing (ACS PA.IV.M.S8) allow touchdown on or within 400 feet beyond the point. Short-field landings allow only 200 feet (ACS PA.IV.F.S10). On a short field, too much airspeed can make you touch down too far down the runway [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
